questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Chitin and glucan in the fungal wall
questions.learningObjective: account for the measured composition of a fungal cell wall
questions.stem: A prepared sample of fungal cell wall weighs 25 milligrams and is 40 percent chitin, 50 percent glucan and 10 percent other material by mass. How much of the sample is chitin?

options.text: 10.0 milligrams, which is 40 percent of the 25 milligrams weighed
12.5 milligrams, which is the glucan fraction rather than the chitin one
options.misconception: reads the glucan percentage as if it applied to the chitin question

options.text: 2.5 milligrams, which is the fraction described as other material
options.misconception: substitutes the residual fraction for the named polymer

options.text: 40 milligrams, which takes the percentage as a mass without multiplying
options.misconception: drops the total mass and treats the percentage figure as grams

questions.explanation: The chitin fraction is 0.40 of the sample, so 0.40 times 25 milligrams is 10.0 milligrams, and by the same route the glucan is 0.50 times 25, which is 12.5 milligrams, and the other material is 0.10 times 25, which is 2.5 milligrams. The three add to 25.0 milligrams, which is the check that the composition has been read correctly. Chitin is a polymer of N-acetylglucosamine that gives the wall its resistance to being stretched and to being digested by most enzymes, while the glucans are the structural framework that the wall actually tears along, and together they are what makes a fungal wall unlike a plant cell wall, which uses cellulose in that role. The exact proportions vary widely between fungal groups and between growth states.
questions.hint: Multiply the percentage by the 25 milligrams, then check that the three parts add back to 25.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a single hypha from the mycelium formed by many of them
questions.stem: A fungus is described as having a body of thread-like tubes branching through its substrate. What are the single tube and the whole branching mass called?

options.text: The single tube is a mycelium and the branching mass is a hypha
options.misconception: reverses the two terms, so the collective body is read as a single thread

options.text: The single tube is a hypha and the branching mass is a mycelium
The single tube is a root hair and the branching mass is a root system
options.misconception: imports plant vocabulary for a body that has no organs or vascular tissue

options.text: The single tube is a frond and the branching mass is a prothallus
options.misconception: uses fern terms, where the names refer to different generations of one plant

questions.explanation: The fungal body plan has two words for its two scales. A hypha is one elongated tube with a wall, and because the tip of a hypha extends while new material is added behind it, a single hypha can be metres long in a fungus spreading through a log. A mycelium is the whole network of hyphae, and it is the unit that absorbs nutrients, since the surface area of a network is enormous compared with its volume. The plant terms fail because a fungal body has no roots, no vascular tissue and no organs, and the fern terms fail because a fern's prothallus is a separate haploid generation rather than part of the same body as the frond.
questions.hint: Ask whether the word names one structure or the whole network.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain what septa achieve while leaving the cytoplasm continuous
questions.stem: A septate fungal hypha is divided by cross walls that each carry a pore. Why leave the pores open rather than sealing every compartment?

options.text: So the hypha can divide by mitosis inside each compartment, as a cell does
options.misconception: gives a coenocytic hypha the compartmental division of a single cell

options.text: So each compartment can build its own wall at a different thickness, as organs do
options.misconception: treats a fungal compartment as an organ with its own specialisation

options.text: So the cytoplasm stays continuous and materials can be distributed along the whole hypha
So the open pores let spores escape into the air when the hypha is damaged
options.misconception: describes a reproductive function for a purely structural feature

questions.explanation: A septum is a cross wall that keeps the two compartments physically separate but not isolated, because the pore connects their cytoplasms. That compromise is what lets a hypha behave as one integrated system: vesicles, nuclei and nutrients move along it, a growing tip can be supplied from anywhere in the network, and a leak in one part can be walled off by plugging the pore without losing the whole hypha. A hypha with no septa at all is described as coenocytic, one cell with many nuclei, and it is common in the earliest-branching fungal groups and in the mould Rhizopus, so the presence or absence of septa is itself a character used in classification. The belief that pores serve spore release fails because spores are made in specialised structures, not at a damaged septum.
questions.hint: Ask what the fungus loses if a long tube is divided into sealed boxes.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: describe the localised mechanism of hyphal extension
questions.stem: A fungal hypha extends only at its very tip, growing several millimetres an hour in good conditions. What is happening at that tip?

options.text: The tip absorbs nutrients from the substrate and converts them directly into wall material
options.misconception: removes the vesicle trafficking and puts synthesis at the uptake step

options.text: The whole hypha lengthens evenly, so the tip simply happens to be where it happens to end
options.misconception: assumes uniform elongation rather than tip-localised growth

options.text: Mitosis at the tip produces new cells that swell, as in a plant meristem
options.misconception: applies a plant meristem model in which cells divide to extend an organ

options.text: Vesicles carrying wall-building enzymes and membrane are delivered to the apex and fuse there

questions.explanation: Fungal extension is a tip-growth process. Just behind the apex sits a cluster of vesicles, held on cytoskeletal cables, and it is fed by a supply centre that channels material forward from the whole hypha. The vesicles carry the enzymes that build wall components and the membrane that has to accompany new wall, and they fuse at the apex, so the wall is laid down and the membrane is expanded in the same place at the same time. Behind the tip, the wall is still yielding and the cell is still extending, and that is where turgor from absorbed water does the pushing. The belief that the whole hypha lengthens evenly fails because only the apex is open for new wall insertion, and the belief that mitosis at the tip extends an organ fails because a hypha is one cell, not a stack of dividing cells.
questions.hint: Ask where the new membrane has to be inserted if the tip alone is getting longer.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Radial colony growth from a spore
questions.learningObjective: compute a colony growth rate from a linear radius series

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): A single spore was placed at the centre of an agar plate and the plate was incubated at a constant temperature. The colony was a circle, and its radius was measured with a scale across the lid at four times. The results were 1.5 millimetres at 20 hours, 4.0 millimetres at 30 hours, 7.0 millimetres at 42 hours and 11.0 millimetres at 58 hours. The same strain on a second plate, measured at the same four times, gave 3.0, 5.5, 8.5 and 12.5 millimetres, and the second series was discarded because the first measurement was taken before the spore had germinated.

questions.stem: Using only the laboratory note, what is the colony's growth rate, and what radius should it reach at 70 hours?

options.text: 0.25 millimetres per minute, which is 360 per day, giving 14.0 millimetres at 70 hours
options.misconception: reads an hourly rate as a per-minute rate, a factor of sixty

options.text: 0.25 millimetres per hour, which is 6.0 per day, giving 14.0 millimetres at 70 hours
0.50 millimetres per hour, which is the rate for diameter rather than radius
options.misconception: doubles the rate by reporting the growth of the measured diameter instead

options.text: 0.23 millimetres per hour, which divides the total radius by the full time rather than by the change
options.misconception: divides the final radius by the elapsed time, which includes the ungerminated lag

questions.explanation: The four measurements lie exactly on a straight line, because the differences are 2.5 millimetres over 10 hours, then 3.0 over 12, then 4.0 over 16, and each of those is 0.25 millimetres per hour. A least-squares fit through the four points returns the same 0.2500, so the rate is not an artefact of one interval. In days that is 6.0 millimetres, and extending from the first measurement, 1.5 plus 0.25 times 50 hours, gives 14.0 millimetres at 70 hours. The value of discarding the second series is that its 20 hour reading was 3.0 millimetres rather than 1.5, so the plate had been contaminated or mislabelled and a rate fitted to it would not describe the first plate.
questions.hint: Take the differences between consecutive readings, then extend the line from the first point.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: compute a cell count from repeated budding generations
questions.stem: A single yeast cell divides by budding, and every cell produced buds again in the next generation. How many cells are present after twelve generations?

options.text: 12, which counts the number of generations rather than the cells produced
options.misconception: reports the number of rounds instead of the population at the end of them

options.text: 13, which adds one cell for each generation rather than doubling
options.misconception: adds one per generation instead of doubling the existing population

options.text: 4096, which is 2 raised to the power of 12
12288, which multiplies by three because a bud carries a bud as well as a mother
options.misconception: treats a bud as adding two cells when it adds only one

questions.explanation: Every cell in the population buds in each generation, so the population doubles at every step and the count after n generations is 2 to the power of n. Doubling from one gives 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048 and 4096 at the twelfth step, which is the same figure reached without algebra. A bud is a new cell, so the mother is replaced by two rather than three, which is why the factor is two and not three. This is the arithmetic behind the reason a culture of yeast can be counted on a plate as a proxy for a very large population, and behind the reason a culture that has been left to reach the top of its growth curve is no longer doubling.
questions.hint: Write out the doublings one to twelve and read off the last value.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain why a fungus changes its growth form with temperature
questions.stem: The fungus Histoplasma grows as branching hyphae in a culture at 25 degrees Celsius but as single cells inside a mammalian body at 37 degrees. What does that switch reveal?

options.text: The genes for both growth forms are present, and temperature and other signals decide which is expressed
The hyphal form is a juvenile stage that the cells outgrow as the organism matures
options.misconception: reads a switch between two cell states as a life stage within one body

options.text: The two forms are two different species that have been given one name by mistake
options.misconception: turns a phenotypic switch into a taxonomic confusion

options.text: The single-cell form arises by hyphae fragmenting, so no genetic switch is involved
options.misconception: attributes a regulated developmental change to mechanical breakage

questions.explanation: Fungal dimorphism is a gene-regulatory switch, and both forms are built by the same genome. In Histoplasma the change from hyphae to yeast cells is triggered by the temperature and by the carbon dioxide and nutrient conditions found inside a body, and it works by changing which transcription factors are active, so a completely different set of genes is expressed and a different wall architecture is built. The switch is not accidental, because an inhaled hyphal spore germinating at body temperature as a yeast is exactly the process that establishes infection. This matters in medicine: a fungus that changes form with temperature is a fungus whose laboratory culture does not represent what it does in a host, which is one reason such organisms are handled specially.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two forms could be made by the same set of genes.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: What places fungi outside the plant kingdom
questions.learningObjective: give the structural evidence that separates fungi from plants
questions.stem: A fungus and a plant are both multicellular, grow by extending their bodies, and store carbohydrate reserves. Set out the three structural differences that argue they are not close relatives, and say which of them the fossil record supports.

options.text: The presence of a cell wall, the absence of chloroplasts, and the growth of a hyphal network
options.misconception: lists two features fungi share with plants and one that plants do not have

options.text: Cellulose rather than chitin in the wall, no stomata, and starch rather than glycogen as the reserve
options.misconception: gives the fungal wall composition to the plant and leaves the two reserves swapped

options.text: Chitin rather than cellulose, no vascular tissue, and no ability to make any organic compound
options.misconception: turns heterotrophy into an inability to make any organic compound at all

options.text: Chitin rather than cellulose in the wall, no chloroplasts, and glycogen rather than starch as the reserve

questions.explanation: Three differences carry most of the weight. The wall is built of chitin, a polymer of N-acetylglucosamine, rather than the cellulose that forms the plant wall, and chitin is the same material found in the exoskeletons of arthropods. Fungi have no chloroplasts and obtain carbon as organic molecules rather than fixing it. And the storage carbohydrate is glycogen, a branched polymer of glucose, rather than the amylopectin and amylose of starch. The chitin finding is the strongest structural evidence, because it is a shared derived character linking fungi to animals rather than to plants, and it is consistent with what the molecular phylogeny now shows, in which fungi and animals sit in a single clade. The first true fungal fossils are of hyphal fragments preserved in amber, consistent with that arrangement.
questions.hint: Look for one wall difference, one nutritional difference and one storage difference.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain why an absorptive body plan needs a very large surface
questions.stem: A fungus digests its food outside its body and then absorbs the products. Why does that strategy require a thread-like body rather than a solid lump?

options.text: A solid lump cannot hold enough water to dissolve its own digestive products
options.misconception: makes absorptive nutrition a question of water capacity rather than surface

options.text: Digestion outside the body is faster only if the organism can move to each patch of food
options.misconception: makes the strategy depend on movement, which fungi do not do

options.text: Only a surface can secrete enzymes and take up products, so a branching network maximises surface per unit volume
Only threads can cross a cell wall, so a lump would be trapped inside its own substrate
options.misconception: invents a physical barrier that the substrate does not present

questions.explanation: Absorptive nutrition puts the digestive machinery outside the organism, which means everything the fungus gains must pass through a boundary. That makes boundary area the quantity that has to be maximised, and the cheapest way to do that is to be thin and long rather than compact, so a network of narrow tubes gives an enormous surface for the volume of material it contains. This is the same geometric problem a plant solves with leaves and root hairs, and the answer is the same shape. It also explains the consequences: a fungus can invade a solid substrate such as a log or a seed coat rather than having to swallow it, and it cannot take in particles at all, since absorption works on dissolved molecules.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the organism has to do all the exchanging with the outside.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain how a saprotroph obtains carbon from dead material
questions.stem: A bracket fungus on a dead tree stump obtains all of its carbon. What sequence of steps makes that possible?

options.text: Sunlight striking the bracket converts the dead wood directly into fungal tissue
options.misconception: credits photosynthesis to an organism that has no chloroplasts

options.text: The dead tissue is engulfed whole and digested inside the fungus, as an animal would
options.misconception: imports an ingestive step that an absorptive organism cannot perform

options.text: The fungus receives sugars from other living trees through contact with their roots
options.misconception: replaces dead tissue with a living host and so describes a parasite

options.text: Enzymes secreted by the hyphae break the dead polymers into small molecules, which are then absorbed

questions.explanation: A saprotroph is a heterotroph living on dead organic matter, and because it cannot swallow its food it has to make the food soluble first. It secretes extracellular enzymes, including cellulases acting on cellulose and oxidative enzymes acting on lignin, the two substances that make plant cell walls so resistant, and the released sugars and smaller fragments are then absorbed through the hyphal wall and used for growth. The consequence for ecosystems is that a large share of the carbon in a forest floor is released by this route, which is why a dead tree supports a food web rather than simply decaying, and why fungi sit at the base of the decomposer chain. The belief that sunlight does the converting fails because no chlorophyll is present anywhere in the organism.
questions.hint: Ask what has to happen to a polymer before it can be absorbed.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: define an obligate biotroph and explain what that requires of the host
questions.stem: Powdery mildews and rusts cannot be grown on a dead laboratory medium, however rich it is, and the plant cells they colonise stay alive and plump. What does that combination require of the parasite?

options.text: It must kill the host cells first, so a dead medium is the only medium it can use
options.misconception: inverts the requirement, since a necrotroph is the one that kills

options.text: It must draw nutrients from living cells, so it has to keep them alive and metabolically active
It must be able to make its own sugars, so the host is only a place to stand
options.misconception: makes the organism autotrophic while keeping the dependency on living tissue

options.text: It must digest the host completely, since any undegraded part would block the hyphae
options.misconception: describes total internal digestion, which is neither a requirement nor a possibility

questions.explanation: An obligate biotroph takes its nutrients from living host cells and cannot complete its life cycle on dead material, which is what makes it obligate. To keep taking nutrients, it must keep the host cells alive and functioning, so it grows at the surface or between cells, sends specialised feeding structures into the host, and suppresses the host's own defences and its programmed cell death. That is why a powdery mildew can be wiped off a leaf: the superficial mycelium does not damage the tissue beneath it much at all, and a necrotroph that kills its host in patches is a different lifestyle with the opposite requirement. Obligate biotrophs are also the reason a fungus group can be difficult to research, since the standard tool of growing an organism on a defined medium is unavailable for them.
questions.hint: Ask what would happen to the food supply if the host cells died.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: The cell wall as a drug target
questions.learningObjective: explain why fungal wall synthesis is a selective drug target
questions.stem: An antifungal drug blocks the enzyme that builds beta-1,3-glucan in a fungal wall, and the fungus dies without the host being harmed. What makes the target selective?

options.text: Animal cells have no cell wall, so the enzyme and its polymer are absent from them
The drug reaches fungal walls faster because fungal walls are thinner than plant walls
options.misconception: invokes a thickness argument in a host that is not a plant

options.text: The enzyme is the same one the host uses, but the drug cannot reach host cells
options.misconception: claims a shared enzyme, which would make the target non-selective by construction

options.text: Fungal walls are made of protein, so blocking them spares the host's carbohydrate wall
options.misconception: misstates the wall chemistry the selectivity depends on

questions.explanation: Selectivity comes from a difference in what the target organism and the host actually have. Beta-1,3-glucan is a load-bearing component of the fungal wall and is made by a fungal enzyme, and an animal cell has neither the polymer nor the enzyme, so blocking it removes an essential structure from the fungus and nothing essential from the host. The same reasoning applies to chitin synthase, and it is why a drug with a narrow fungal target is preferable to one that acts on a shared pathway. The weakness of the strategy is equally clear: because a growing fungus is not the only thing that needs a wall, the drug is most active on actively dividing cells, which is why the response can take days to appear even when the drug reaches the fungus quickly.
questions.hint: Ask whether the host has the structure being attacked, and how fungi differ from animals in having one.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain how ergosterol gives azoles selectivity over the host
questions.stem: Fungal membranes contain ergosterol, while animal membranes contain cholesterol. An azole drug blocks the enzyme that makes ergosterol. How does blocking it harm the fungus but not the host?

options.text: Ergosterol is made from plant sterols, so a plant host is affected before the fungus is
options.misconception: assigns the fungal sterol a plant origin and inverts the host relationship

options.text: Cholesterol is more fluid than ergosterol, so blocking the fungus's sterol makes it stiffer than the host
options.misconception: compares the two sterols as if the host were the one being stiffened

options.text: The drug dissolves in water, so it reaches fungal membranes faster than host membranes
options.misconception: makes solubility the source of selectivity rather than the target

options.text: The enzyme it blocks is absent from the host, so the host's own sterol synthesis is untouched

questions.explanation: The selective step is the enzyme, not the sterol. The azole class inhibits the fungal enzyme that demethylates lanosterol on the way to ergosterol, and mammals do not make ergosterol and do not carry that enzyme, so their cholesterol synthesis is unaffected. The fungus, meanwhile, runs out of ergosterol and the membrane loses the stability that the sterol provides, which becomes fatal. Interference with other fungal enzymes accounts for a second part of the effect, because the same drugs inhibit the enzyme that uses squalene to make squalene epoxide. A polyene drug works differently, by binding the fungal sterol and puncturing the membrane, and that too is selective because the host's sterol is a different molecule. The point generalises: a drug is selective when its target is absent from the host.
questions.hint: Ask whether the host has the enzyme the drug inhibits, not only the molecule it makes.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: compute a concentration in the original suspension from a plated dilution

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): A suspension of fungal conidia was diluted in tenfold steps. From each dilution 0.1 millilitres was spread over an agar plate and the plates were incubated under identical conditions before being counted. The plate from the ten to the minus three dilution gave 1270 colonies, the plate from the ten to the minus four dilution gave 128 colonies and the plate from the ten to the minus five dilution gave 14 colonies. All three plates were treated identically and each was counted once.

questions.stem: Using only the laboratory note, which plate should be used, and what concentration in the original suspension does it imply?

options.text: The 128 colony plate, giving 128 divided by 10 to the minus 4, or 1.28 x 10 to the 6 per millilitre
options.misconception: forgets that only 0.1 millilitres was spread, not the whole dilution

options.text: The 128 colony plate, giving 128 divided by 10 to the minus 5 millilitres, or 1.28 x 10 to the 7 per millilitre
The 14 colony plate, giving 14 divided by 10 to the minus 5, or 1.4 x 10 to the 7 per millilitre
options.misconception: uses a plate below the countable range, where the error is largest

options.text: The 1270 colony plate, giving 1270 divided by 10 to the minus 3, or 1.27 x 10 to the 7 per millilitre
options.misconception: uses a plate above the countable range, where colonies merge

questions.explanation: A plate is only usable when the colonies are far enough apart to be counted and numerous enough for the count to be reliable, which conventionally means between 30 and 300. The 128 colony plate is the only one in that range. The 0.1 millilitres spread from the ten to the minus four dilution is equivalent to 0.1 times 10 to the minus 4, which is 10 to the minus 5, millilitres of the original suspension, and 128 colonies in that volume is 128 times 10 to the 5, which is 1.28 x 10 to the 7 per millilitre. The three plates agree well, giving 1.27 x 10 to the 7, 1.28 x 10 to the 7 and 1.4 x 10 to the 7, all within about a tenth of one another, so the answer is not sensitive to which of the near values is reported.
questions.hint: The volume plated is not the same as the volume of the dilution, so convert both before dividing.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: The countable range on a plate
questions.learningObjective: state why plates outside 30 to 300 colonies are not used
questions.stem: A plate with 18 colonies and one with 640 colonies are both rejected while a plate with 128 is accepted. What makes the middle plate the reliable one?

options.text: Above 30 the agar is thick enough to hold them and below 300 the dish is not overloaded
options.misconception: explains the range by the physical capacity of the plate

options.text: Above 30 the colonies are large enough to see, and below 300 they have not yet spread
options.misconception: moves the bounds onto colony size rather than separability and count

options.text: Above 30 the sampling error falls, and below 300 neighbouring colonies have not begun to merge
Above 30 the incubation is long enough to grow them and below 300 no strain change occurs
options.misconception: attributes the limit to the incubation rather than to the counting

questions.explanation: The two ends of the range fail for opposite reasons, and both are about reliability rather than about the plate. At the low end, the number of colonies is a small sample, so the same suspension gives very different counts on replicate plates, and a relative error of a few colonies is a large fraction of a small total. At the high end, colonies touch and merge, so what is counted is clumps of cells rather than separate colony-forming units, and the count under-reports. Between roughly 30 and 300 the count is both reproducible and separable, which is why the convention exists. It is a convention rather than a law, and a wider spread of acceptable values is sometimes used for very dilute suspensions, but the reasoning above is what it encodes.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of error grows at each end: sampling error, or colonies running together.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Counting cells on a counting chamber
questions.learningObjective: convert a chamber count into a concentration in the original sample
questions.stem: A suspension was diluted one part in twenty before loading. Counting chamber squares of 1 square millimetre with a chamber depth of 0.1 millimetres gave 32 cells in four squares. What is the concentration in the original suspension?

options.text: 1.6 x 10 to the 6 cells per millilitre, from 32 cells in 4 x 10 to the minus 4 millilitres
8.0 x 10 to the 4 cells per millilitre, which is the count before the dilution is undone
options.misconception: reports the concentration of the diluted suspension rather than the original

options.text: 1.6 x 10 to the 5 cells per millilitre, which applies the dilution in the wrong direction
options.misconception: divides by twenty when the twenty should multiply

options.text: 3.2 x 10 to the 7 cells per millilitre, which counts each square as if it held a tenth
options.misconception: applies a spurious tenth to the chamber depth

questions.explanation: The volume under one square is the area times the depth, so 1 square millimetre is 10 to the minus 6 square metres and 0.1 millimetres is 10 to the minus 4 metres, giving 10 to the minus 10 cubic metres, which is 10 to the minus 4 millilitres. Four squares therefore hold 4 x 10 to the minus 4, or 0.0004 millilitres, and 32 cells in that volume is 32 divided by 0.0004, which is 8.0 x 10 to the 4 per millilitre of the diluted suspension. The dilution was one part in twenty, so the original is twenty times that, which is 1.6 x 10 to the 6 per millilitre. A second chamber giving 30 cells in the same four squares would give 1.5 x 10 to the 6, close enough to support the figure.
questions.hint: Turn the area and the depth into a volume first, then undo the dilution last.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Doubling time from two cell counts
questions.learningObjective: compute a doubling time from two counts and a time interval
questions.stem: A culture holds 2.0 x 10 to the 6 cells per millilitre at time zero and 6.4 x 10 to the 7 at 3.0 hours, with no lag and no stationary phase in between. What is the doubling time?

options.text: 180 minutes, which divides the interval by the number of doublings the wrong way round
options.misconception: is the whole interval, as though one doubling had taken the full time

options.text: 18 minutes, which counts the thirty-two-fold rise as ten doublings rather than five
options.misconception: treats a factor of two as ten doublings instead of five

options.text: 36 minutes, from a thirty-two-fold rise being five doublings in 3.0 hours
60 minutes, which is the interval per doubling if the rise were taken as a factor of three
options.misconception: reads the fold increase as three rather than thirty-two

questions.explanation: The population rose by a factor of 6.4 x 10 to the 7 over 2.0 x 10 to the 6, which is 32, and 32 is 2 to the power of 5, so the culture doubled five times in 3.0 hours. Three hours divided by five doublings is 0.60 hours, which is 36 minutes. The same figure comes from the natural logarithm route: the specific growth rate is the natural log of 32 over 3.0 hours, which is 1.155 per hour, and one doubling time is the natural log of two divided by that, which is 0.600 hours. As a check, the count predicted at 1.8 hours is 2.0 x 10 to the 6 times 2 to the power of 3, which is 1.6 x 10 to the 7, and running forward from there for the remaining 1.2 hours, which is two more doublings, returns 6.4 x 10 to the 7.
questions.hint: Convert the fold change into a number of doublings before dividing the time by it.

questions.stem: A culture's dry mass rose from 0.40 to 1.60 grams in 12.0 hours, and in another flask 8.6 grams of dry biomass was produced from 20.0 grams of glucose. What are the doubling time and the biomass yield?

options.text: 3.0 hours and 0.43 grams, which uses three doublings for a four-fold rise
options.misconception: counts the four-fold rise as three doublings instead of two

options.text: 6.0 hours and 0.43 grams of biomass per gram of glucose
6.0 hours and 2.33 grams, which divides the glucose by the biomass rather than the reverse
options.misconception: inverts the yield ratio and reports substrate per product

options.text: 24.0 hours and 0.43 grams, which uses the whole interval as one doubling
options.misconception: ignores that the mass quadrupled, so two doublings occurred

questions.explanation: The dry mass went from 0.40 to 1.60 grams, a factor of 4, and a factor of 4 is 2 to the power of 2, so there were two doublings in 12.0 hours and the doubling time is 6.0 hours. Working back the other way, 0.40 times 2 to the power of 12.0 divided by 6.0 returns exactly 1.60 grams, which confirms the figure. The yield is biomass produced divided by substrate consumed, so 8.6 divided by 20.0 is 0.43 grams of biomass per gram of glucose, meaning 43 percent of the substrate mass ended up as cell material and the rest went on to other products or to carbon dioxide. Using dry mass rather than wet mass matters because wet mass is mostly water and would make the growth rate meaningless.
questions.hint: A four-fold rise is two doublings, and a yield is product over substrate.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: survey the asexual propagules a fungus may produce
questions.stem: A fungus can spread without any mating at all. Which of these is one way it does so?

options.text: It fragments a hypha at a septum, and the pieces each continue growing as new mycelia
options.misconception: labels fragmentation as spore formation when no spore is involved

options.text: It fuses two hyphae of the same strain and forms a dikaryotic mycelium by plasmogamy
options.misconception: describes the start of a sexual cycle as if it were an asexual route

options.text: It forms a zygote in which the two nuclei finally fuse to make a diploid spore
options.misconception: moves the sexual cycle one step later while still calling it asexual

options.text: It releases asexual spores from a specialised structure, each of which grows into a new mycelium

questions.explanation: Asexual reproduction makes a genetically identical copy without any fusion of two nuclei, and it takes several forms. Asexual spores are produced in a fruiting body and released to germinate directly, and they are the main way a fungal species disperses, which is why a single fruiting body can seed a whole area. Budding in yeasts is the same idea at the level of the single cell, with a new cell emerging from a bud that separates and repeats. Fragmentation of a mycelium is also genuinely asexual, and it is why an old mushroom culture can regenerate from a scrap of agar. The belief that plasmogamy is asexual fails because fusing two strains is the beginning of a sexual cycle even though the nuclei stay apart at that stage.
questions.hint: Ask whether any two nuclei or cells had to come together to make the new individual.

questions.learningObjective: describe how a sporangium releases its spores
questions.stem: In a mould such as Rhizopus, a swollen tip of an aerial hypha fills with spores and the whole tip then bursts. What is the advantage of packaging spores that way?

Many spores are made in one place and released in a single event, so dispersal is efficient rather than one spore at a time, and until the moment of release the spores sit inside a protected cavity rather than exposed on the surface of the mycelium. The spores inside a sporangium are made by mitosis from a diploid nucleus, so they are haploid and genetically identical to the parent, which is what makes the structure an asexual one. The burst itself is driven by the uptake of water into the swelling vesicle, so it is a change in turgor rather than an active throwing action, and the pressure of the break is what throws the spores clear.
questions.hint: Ask what is gained by putting many spores inside one cavity before they go anywhere.

questions.stem: Many plant pathogens, such as the moulds that rot a citrus fruit, produce dry spores in chains on upright stalks. What does that arrangement achieve?

Carrying them in chains at the top of an upright stalk puts a large number of small particles high above the leaf, which is exactly the design that lets air currents and rain splash pick them up and move them. The arrangement is the opposite of a sporangium, which encloses its spores until it bursts. The belief that the spores need water to swim fails because that is a different structure in a different group, the motile zoospore.

questions.learningObjective: describe a second route to a new asexual individual
questions.stem: A hypha laid across a plate breaks up into short segments, and each segment carries on growing as a new colony. What has produced those colonies?

Mating between two adjacent segments, which fused before they separated

options.misconception: substitutes spore production for simple breakage of existing tissue

questions.explanation: Fragmentation is the simplest form of asexual reproduction: a mycelium breaks at its septa and every fragment that is large enough to carry on becomes a new individual with the same genotype. Because the fragments are already colonised, the process is fast, which is why an old culture left on a plate produces new colonies where it touched, and why transferring material with a wire loop can seed a fresh plate with either a spore or a scrap of hypha. It is also the practical reason fungi survive handling: a colony that would be killed as a single delicate structure survives as many separate pieces. What fragmentation does not involve is any change in chromosome number, so the pieces are vegetative rather than reproductive in the strict sense.

questions.learningObjective: define the dikaryotic phase and say what it is for
questions.stem: Two compatible hyphae fuse so that their cytoplasms mix, but the nuclei from each stay separate and divide side by side. What has been produced, and why does the fungus keep it that way?

options.text: A haploid mycelium, kept single-set so that the offspring are identical to one parent
options.misconception: describes one parent rather than a stable pairing of two

options.text: A diploid mycelium, kept two sets of chromosomes so that the offspring differ from both parents
options.misconception: calls the dikaryon diploid and gives it the wrong source of variation

options.text: A dikaryotic mycelium, kept n plus n so that two parental genotypes persist before any fusion of nuclei
A triploid mycelium, kept three sets so that the extra set can be lost at germination
options.misconception: borrows the ploidy of a later tissue and attaches it to the vegetative phase

questions.explanation: Plasmogamy merges the cytoplasm of two cells while karyogamy, the fusion of nuclei, is held in reserve. The mycelium that results carries two haploid nuclei, one from each parent, side by side in every compartment, with the nuclear pairing maintained by clamp connections in the basidiomycetes. Keeping them apart for this long has a consequence: the two genomes are carried together in one body, so a new sexual structure can be built with a mixed parentage, and recombination can happen in the basidium when the two nuclei finally fuse and then undergo meiosis. The phase is called dikaryotic precisely to record that there are two separate nuclei rather than one set of paired chromosomes, and it is a stage no plant has.

questions.topic: Karyogamy and the return to haploidy
questions.learningObjective: sequence the events that turn a dikaryon back into haploid spores
questions.stem: Deep inside a mushroom, two nuclei in one basidium fuse, and the nucleus that results divides twice more. What is the state of the nuclei that the divisions produce?

options.text: Triploid, because the basidium supplies a third set to the fused nucleus
options.misconception: adds a third set to a fusion that combines exactly two

options.text: Diploid, because the first fusion doubled the set and the divisions only partition it
options.misconception: stops after the fusion and ignores the meiotic divisions that follow it

options.text: Dikaryotic, because each of the four nuclei is a separate product of the original pair
options.misconception: calls the four products a pair, which is what dikaryotic names

options.text: Haploid, because the fused diploid nucleus is halved twice by the second and third divisions

questions.explanation: The fusion of the two nuclei produces a diploid nucleus, and what follows is meiosis, so the two subsequent divisions restore haploidy. That is the whole point of the arrangement: the dikaryotic phase can be maintained indefinitely without any nuclear fusion, and the fusion is deferred to a single cell where the genetic consequences can be contained. Each of the four products then behaves as a new starting nucleus, and in the basidiomycetes each migrates to a small stalk and becomes a basidiospore on its own. The belief that the four products are dikaryotic fails because dikaryotic describes a pairing of two nuclei within a compartment, and there is only one nucleus per compartment at this point.
questions.hint: Count the chromosome sets before the fusion and after each of the two following divisions.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: state what a clamp connection maintains
questions.stem: A hypha of a mushroom shows short hook-shaped bridges that wrap from one cell across the septum to the cell beyond. What do those bridges maintain?

options.text: A continuous hollow lumen, by holding the two cell walls open across every septum
options.misconception: makes a cytoplasmic bridge into a passage for water and dissolved solutes

options.text: The dikaryotic condition, by keeping one nucleus of each parent in every compartment as the hypha grows
The wall thickness, by reinforcing the septum where the two new cells meet
options.misconception: reads a reproductive structure as a mechanical one

options.text: The haploid state, by preventing the two nuclei from ever meeting and fusing
options.misconception: inverts the function, since the structure exists because fusion is being deferred, not prevented

questions.explanation: A clamp connection is a feature of the dikaryotic phase. When a compartment containing two nuclei divides, the new septum would otherwise leave one compartment with both nuclei and the other with none, so the parent cell grows a hook that puts a nucleus into each daughter and reconnects them. The result is that every compartment of the hypha holds exactly one nucleus of each parental genotype, indefinitely, and the connection is the visible evidence of that bookkeeping. It is the reason a mushroom's flesh is a dikaryotic mycelium rather than a single set of cells, and it is a character used to tell fungal groups apart. The belief that the bridge is a water conduit fails because the pore in the septum already does that job, whether or not a clamp is present.
questions.hint: Ask what would go wrong at the next division if one compartment received both nuclei.

options.misconception: adds a generation of division that is not part of the sequence

options.text: Four, which counts the products of the meiosis and forgets the extra mitosis
options.misconception: stops at the end of the meiosis

Two, which counts the two nuclei produced by the first meiotic division alone

questions.learningObjective: state how many spores a basidium bears and where they sit

An ascus, and it holds eight spores inside the sac before they are released
options.misconception: borrows the sac and the count of an ascomycete structure

options.text: A basidium, and it bears spores in chains above the tip as a conidiophore does
options.misconception: gives a basidium the chain-bearing arrangement of a conidiophore

options.text: A sporangium, and it releases several hundred spores at once when its wall breaks
options.misconception: describes a bursting sporangium rather than a cell with fixed spore-bearing tips

Four is the standard number and the exceptions are few enough to be treated as special cases rather than as the rule. Because the spores are launched from a surface rather than dropped, a single mushroom can throw its spores a measurable distance, and the four-by-four arrangement on a cap face is the basis of the counting estimate in the next item.

questions.topic: The sexual cycle as an ordering
questions.learningObjective: order the sexual cycle of a mushroom from plasmogamy to spore discharge
questions.stem: Arrange these five events in the sequence that makes up the sexual cycle of a mushroom-forming fungus.

options.text: Two compatible haploid spores germinate and their hyphae grow towards each other
The hyphae fuse, cytoplasms mix and a dikaryotic mycelium is established with clamp connections
Fruiting bodies develop at the surface where the two parental strains meet
In each basidium the two nuclei fuse and then undergo two meiotic divisions
Four basidiospores form on the basidium and are discharged from the gill surface

questions.explanation: The cycle is ordered by where each event happens in space and time. Two spores land near each other, germinate, and the two germ tubes recognise each other because of the mating type carried by each nucleus, and they fuse. The dikaryotic mycelium so formed has to grow, sometimes for years, before it is ready to fruit, and fruiting bodies appear where the two parental mycelia meet, which is why the shape of a mushroom's cap records the meeting point. Only then, inside each basidium, do the two nuclei fuse and undergo meiosis, and the four products become four spores that are launched from the gill. Fusion of the nuclei last, after fruiting, is what makes the cycle unusual among organisms.
questions.hint: Fusion of the nuclei happens later than fusion of the hyphae, and both happen before fruiting.

questions.learningObjective: explain why lignin breakdown limits what can be decomposed
questions.stem: Cellulose can be broken down by many organisms, but lignin resists almost all of them, and a wood-rotting fungus that clears a fallen trunk is the exception. What does that tell you about lignin?

options.misconception: makes lignin a mineral, which it is not

options.text: It is a soluble sugar that binds to the cellulose and makes the whole wall taste bitter
options.misconception: describes lignin as a soluble molecule rather than an insoluble polymer

options.text: It is a tough, cross-linked phenolic polymer that most organisms lack the enzymes to attack
It is an enzyme secreted by the plant to defend itself against fungal attack

questions.explanation: Lignin is a three-dimensional network of phenolic units, mostly phenylpropanoid in origin, that permeates the cell walls of secondary xylem and is covalently bonded to the carbohydrate matrix. Its cross-linking is what gives wood its rigidity, and the same cross-linking is what makes it so hard to break, because an enzyme that cleaves one bond in the network still leaves the material in one piece. Animals have no mechanism for degrading it at all, which is why lignin is indigestible and appears as dietary fibre, and it is also why the carbon locked in lignin is the fraction that decomposes most slowly. The fungi that do clear wood achieve it with extracellular oxidative enzymes and, in the brown rot fungi, with a non-enzymatic route that generates free radicals, which is a genuinely different chemistry rather than a stronger version of the same one.

questions.topic: Nutrient transfer in a mycorrhizal plant
questions.learningObjective: compute the percentage gain in phosphorus from a mycorrhizal inoculation

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): Fifteen seedlings of one species were grown in pots of the same sterile soil with the same fertiliser. The first group of three received no fungal inoculum, the second group of six received a standard arbuscular inoculum, and the third group of six received the same inoculum that had been killed by autoclaving. After eight weeks each plant's shoot phosphorus was measured in milligrams and the results were recorded. Uninoculated plants: 11.0, 12.0 and 10.0. Live-inoculum plants: 19.0, 20.0 and 21.0, with two further values recorded but not supplied. Autoclaved-inoculum plants: 11.0, 12.0 and 12.0. Every pot received the same volume of water and the same light.

questions.stem: Using only the laboratory note, how much does the live inoculum raise the shoot phosphorus, and what does the autoclaved control add?

options.text: 9.0 milligrams, an 81.8 percent rise, and the autoclaved control shows the live fungus is what does it
9.0 milligrams, an 18.2 percent rise, which divides the gain by the inoculated mean instead
options.misconception: divides the gain by the treated group, which understates the benefit

options.text: 2.0 milligrams, a rise of about 18 percent, which compares the two inoculated groups with each other
options.misconception: subtracts the uninoculated mean from the autoclaved mean instead

options.text: 10.0 milligrams, a doubling, which compares the inoculated mean with the lowest uninoculated value
options.misconception: uses a single extreme control reading as though it were the group mean

questions.explanation: The uninoculated mean is 11 plus 12 plus 10 over 3, which is 11.0, and the live-inoculum mean is 19 plus 20 plus 21 over 3, which is 20.0, so the gain is 9.0 milligrams and as a percentage of the untreated mean that is 9.0 divided by 11.0, which is 81.8. Written as a ratio instead, 20.0 divided by 11.0 is 1.818, and 1.818 minus 1 is the same 81.8 percent. The autoclaved group is the decisive addition to the design: its mean is 11 plus 12 plus 12 over 3, which is 11.7, close to the uninoculated mean, so the benefit is not from any component of the inoculum that survives heating but from the living fungus. Two further values from the live group are withheld, and they could only change the size of the effect, not the conclusion that it is large and needs the living fungus.
questions.hint: Compare the treated mean with the untreated mean, then check what the killed-inoculum control does.

The fungus supplies the housing, the absorbed water and minerals, and the protection from desiccation that lets the photosynthetic partner survive at all. The two are not interchangeable and neither is complete without the other, which is why lichen thalli are named for both partners, such as the form of the algal cells described as a trebouxioid.

Enumerating the pairs instead gives the same figure: there are 900 times 100, or 90 000, compatible unordered pairs out of 1000 times 999 divided by 2, which is 499 500 pairs in all, and 90 000 over 499 500 is 18.02 percent. The two routes differ only in whether an individual is allowed to be drawn twice, and both round to 18.0 percent. The biological reading is that mating between members of the same type is blocked by a mechanism that acts on the mating type genes, so a single mating type allele system keeps a population from self-fertilising and makes recombination between strains possible.
questions.hint: Compatible means one of each, so add the two possible orders of the same product.

questions.stem: Two isolates of one species are grown on the same medium for 48 hours. Isolate M reaches a radius of 10.0 millimetres and isolate P reaches 20.0. How much faster is P, and when will P reach 30 millimetres?

options.misconception: adds the two radii before dividing rather than dividing each

options.text: Twice as fast at 10.0 millimetres per day, and P reaches 30 millimetres at 72 hours
Twice as fast at 5.0 millimetres per day, and P reaches 30 millimetres at 144 hours

options.text: Ten times as fast at 20.0 millimetres per day, and P reaches 30 millimetres at 72 hours

questions.learningObjective: compute product yields and check the carbon closes
questions.stem: A fermenter fed 100 grams of glucose yields 40 grams of dry biomass, 30 grams of ethanol and 30 grams of carbon dioxide. What are the two product yields, and does the carbon account for the feed?

options.misconception: inverts both yields and reports substrate per product

0.40 and 0.30 grams per gram, but the outputs come to 70 grams and 30 grams is missing

options.text: 0.70 and 0.30 grams per gram, which sums the biomass and ethanol into one yield
options.misconception: merges two distinct products into a single yield

questions.explanation: A yield is product over substrate, so the biomass yield is 40 divided by 100, which is 0.40 grams of biomass per gram of glucose, and the ethanol yield is 30 divided by 100, which is 0.30. The carbon closes: 40 plus 30 plus 30 is 100 grams, so every gram of feed is accounted for across the three outputs, with 40 percent of the feed's mass in cell material, 30 percent in ethanol and 30 percent as gas. The comparison to draw is with the pure fermentation case, where the theoretical maximum ethanol yield is 0.5114 grams per gram of glucose, so this culture is well short of that because a substantial share of the sugar is being spent on growing cells instead. That trade is the whole basis of using the same organism for food and for fuel.
questions.hint: Divide each product by the feed, then add all three products and compare with the feed.

questions.topic: An error in a colony count
questions.learningObjective: identify a unit error in a reported concentration
questions.stem: A student counts 128 colonies on a plate inoculated with 0.1 millilitres of a ten to the minus four dilution of a fungal suspension, and reports 1.28 x 10 to the 6 per millilitre. What is the error?

options.text: The temperature of incubation was not stated, so the result cannot be checked at all
options.misconception: demands a control variable the calculation does not depend on

options.text: The dilution was applied twice, because the plate was already labelled ten to the minus four
options.misconception: invents a second dilution step that the protocol does not describe

options.text: The volume plated was ignored, so the count was divided by the dilution rather than by the volume times the dilution
The colonies were counted on the wrong side of the plate, so the figure should be doubled
options.misconception: suggests a systematic doubling that no count of one plate would justify

questions.explanation: A concentration is colonies divided by the amount of original suspension that reached the plate, and the amount plated was 0.1 millilitres of the ten to the minus four dilution, which is 0.1 times 10 to the minus 4, or 10 to the minus 5, millilitres of the original. So 128 divided by 10 to the minus 5 is 1.28 x 10 to the 7 per millilitre, and the reported figure is low by a factor of ten because the 0.1 disappeared from the denominator. This is the commonest error in any dilution calculation and it is easy to catch by writing the denominator as a number of millilitres before converting. The reported value is also internally inconsistent with the sister plates in the same series, which implied 1.27 x 10 to the 7 and 1.4 x 10 to the 7, so the series itself flagged the error.
questions.hint: Write down how many millilitres of the original suspension actually reached the plate.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Testing whether a trait is fungal rather than plant-made
questions.learningObjective: design a test that attributes a structural trait to the fungal partner
questions.stem: A lichen's outer surface is claimed to be made of fungal material rather than of the photosynthetic partner. Describe an experiment that would test the claim, and say what the result would mean.

answer.exemplar: The claim is about which of two organisms makes a structure, so the design has to separate the two genomes. A staining and microscopy approach does it directly: a thin section of the thallus treated with a stain for the fungal wall polysaccharide, compared with a section of pure fungal material and a section of the isolated photobiont grown on its own, all processed identically and read under the same microscope. If the fungal stain lights up the outer layer and not the inner algal cells, and matches the pure fungal control, the claim is supported. A second, stronger line of evidence separates the organisms genetically: sequence the messenger RNA present in the thallus and ask which of the two partner genomes the transcripts came from, since a transcript cannot be made by a genome that is not there. The controls that matter are the two pure controls, because they set what each partner looks like alone, and the unmixed growth of both partners on the same medium, which shows whether the association is required for either to make the structure. The limits should be stated: this establishes which partner's material is present in which layer, not that the structure is unnecessary, since both organisms may contribute to building it jointly.

questions.explanation: Two independent lines of evidence are worth designing here. Histochemical staining of a thallus section, read against sections of each partner grown alone, can show that the stainable material lies in the fungal layer rather than in the algal cells. And a sequence of the messenger RNA present in the thallus can attribute the transcripts to one partner's genome, since a transcript can only be made from a gene that is present, which is a direct answer to which organism is transcribing there. The crucial controls are the pure cultures of each partner and the growth of both partners separately under the same conditions, because without them a positive staining result could simply reflect the stain's own specificity. A negative result on the isolated photobiont is what makes the outer layer's attribution meaningful rather than merely consistent.
questions.hint: Compare the mixed structure with each partner grown alone under identical conditions.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Testing that a symbiotic partner supplies a nutrient
questions.learningObjective: design a test that separates a symbiotic nutrient transfer from a general growth effect
questions.stem: A plant inoculated with a mycorrhizal fungus grows better in soil with little available phosphate. Describe an experiment that would test whether the fungus is delivering the phosphate, rather than simply stimulating the plant some other way.

answer.exemplar: The difficulty is that a bigger plant has taken up more of everything, so measuring plant growth alone cannot distinguish a delivered nutrient from a general stimulation. The design therefore has to measure the nutrient itself and to put the fungus where the phosphate is not. First, label the phosphate in the soil with a tracer and follow it: grow inoculated and uninoculated plants in soil whose phosphate is labelled, then measure the labelled phosphate in the plant tissue and, in a parallel set of pots, the labelled phosphate in the fungus. Label moving into the plant from a labelled fungal compartment is direct evidence of transfer rather than inference. Second, use a physical separation that a hypha can cross and water cannot: grow the plant in one compartment of a divided pot with its roots, the fungus in the other with the phosphate, so the only route between them is fungal and the two cannot share soil or root contact. If the plant still gains labelled phosphate in that arrangement, the fungus is the only possible route. The constants that matter are equal light, temperature, pot volume and watering, and the necessity of a killed-inoculum control, since a preparation that has been autoclaved may still carry soluble compounds that boost growth. What would undermine the claim is a benefit in the divided pot where the fungus is absent, since that would show the effect is not fungal transfer at all.

questions.explanation: The general form of this experiment is that a growth effect and a nutrient transfer effect must be made to look different. A labelled nutrient in the fungal compartment, isolated from the root compartment by a barrier that only hyphae can cross, turns the inference into a measurement: if the plant tissue acquires label, the fungus carried it. A whole-plant growth response alone does not do this, because a fungus that merely alters root architecture or hormone signalling would produce the same result, and a bigger plant accumulates more of every nutrient. The killed-inoculum control is essential, because an autoclaved fungal preparation releases soluble compounds and the growth effect would then be present without any living fungus. The honest conclusion is bounded to the mechanism that was tested, and the two-part arrangement is what keeps the test specific rather than general.
questions.hint: Make the nutrient measurable and make the only route from it to the plant run through the fungus.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Why fungi are placed in their own kingdom
questions.learningObjective: explain the evidence for and the limits of separating the fungi
questions.stem: Fungi are treated as a kingdom of their own, separate from plants and separate from animals. Explain what evidence supports that treatment, and say what would count against it.

answer.exemplar: The strongest structural evidence is the wall. A fungal wall is built on chitin, a polymer of N-acetylglucosamine, where a plant wall is built on cellulose, and chitin is also the material of the arthropod exoskeleton. That single character points away from the plants and towards the animals, and it is a shared derived feature rather than a shared primitive one, which is what makes it informative about relationships. Three further characters support the same reading: fungi are heterotrophs with no chloroplasts, they store glycogen where plants store starch, and they digest food outside the body and absorb it, which no plant does. A fourth is unique to them: the dikaryotic phase, in which two haploid nuclei from different parents persist side by side in every compartment of a mycelium for as long as that mycelium lives, held in place by clamp connections. Molecular phylogeny agrees, placing fungi together with animals and the slime moulds in one clade and away from the plants. The honest qualification is that a kingdom is a human decision about rank rather than a fact about nature, and it is revisable. What would count against the current arrangement is evidence that the chitin wall and the heterotrophic nutrition are ancestral to a larger group, in which case fungi might be better described as a lineage within something broader. A single organism with a chitin wall and photosynthesis, or a group that shares the fungi's distinctive cell biology but not the wall, would push in that direction, and the strongest form of the argument is that a classification should be revised when it stops predicting which characters travel together.

questions.explanation: The claim rests on a combination of characters rather than on one. The wall chemistry is the most informative single difference, because chitin links fungi to the arthropod exoskeleton and away from the cellulose of plants. Nutrition and storage differ in the directions those two related groups differ, heterotrophy and glycogen rather than autotrophy and starch. And the dikaryotic phase is a developmental arrangement no plant has, in which two haploid nuclei are held in every compartment of the growing body for months or years before any fusion. Molecular phylogeny supports the same grouping, which is what makes the arrangement defensible rather than arbitrary. The evidence against would be a demonstration that these characters are ancestral rather than derived, and the discipline in such a claim is to say that a kingdom is a rank chosen by people and therefore revisable, rather than to present the arrangement as settled.
questions.hint: Lead with the wall chemistry, then say what a shared derived character implies about relationships.
